extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of comparative religion, mythology, folklore, and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical standards for analysing methods, evidence, and arguments in comparative religion, mythological and folklore studies. Emphasises data quality, method choice (comparative vs adjacent), interpretation cautions, and how to treat myths, ritual, and written tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in etymological interpretation of proper/local/mythical names
rubrics_metrics.description: It is especially difficult to conjecture the meaning of proper names, and above all of local and mythical names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid facile or confident etymological derivations across languages (e.g., non-Greek names). Recognize limits of philological conjecture when dealing with names from unfamiliar languages or cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer anthropological/contextual methods for myths and ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of the anthropological school is vindicated over purely philological methods in the explanation of various myths and ritualistic customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contextual, ethnographic, and anthropological evidence (ritual context, social function) rather than relying solely on textual/philological analysis to explain myths and rituals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require adequate knowledge of supernatural beliefs before applying them
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology can scarcely concern itself where our knowledge of the supernatural is by no means sufficient to permit us to apply it to anthropology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not build anthropological theories on an inadequate understanding of the supernatural concepts in the cultures studied; gather sufficient data on local beliefs before drawing comparative conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for post-contact missionary or theological modification
rubrics_metrics.description: The religious ideas of the races alluded to as monotheistic may have been modified by the theology of missionaries, Christian or Mohammedan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting apparent monotheism or other theological features in 'primitive' societies, explicitly consider missionary influence and post-contact changes; test claims of antiquity against contact-history evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require extensive, rigorous data before proposing sweeping theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Before [Lang's theory] can be discussed in its entirety, the religious ideas of the peoples ... will require to be much more fully and rigorously examined and a much larger body of data collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat revolutionary or wide-ranging claims as provisional until supported by broad, rigorous comparative data; avoid generalising from small or unrepresentative samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-inference conditions (Frazer's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we can show that a barbarous custom has existed elsewhere; detect the motives which led to its institution; prove that these motives have operated widely ... and show that these motives were actually at work in classical antiquity, then we may fairly infer that at a remoter age the same motives gave birth to the custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring historical origins by analogy, satisfy these conditions: (1) demonstrate analogous customs elsewhere, (2) identify the motivating causes, (3) show the causes operated widely, (4) find evidence of the same motives in the target culture; the probability of inference depends on how completely these are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overrigid 'stratification' periodisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The criticism that Frazer leans too much to the side of the 'stratification' theory--the belief in the existence of certain fixed religious conditions at different epochs...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of labeling fixed 'ages' (e.g., 'age of magic') or treating stages as mutually exclusive; acknowledge overlap and coexistence of religious types and regional variation rather than imposing strict chronological strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance universal comparative and 'adjacent' (local) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir James Frazer is accused of employing the universal comparative method at the expense of the 'adjacent' method, the method which studies the religion of a certain people in its own sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both comparative (wide analogies) and adjacent/local (in-depth, contextual) approaches suitably. Recognise that comparative work often relies on secondhand sources, but combine it with close, culture-specific study where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't confuse resemblance with identity; distinguish differences
rubrics_metrics.description: He possesses the faculty of seeing resemblances but not differences when dealing with analogies, and that, consequently, he lumps too many diverse facts together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing analogies, explicitly seek and articulate dissimilarities as well as similarities; avoid indiscriminate lumping of diverse phenomena under a single explanatory label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow arguments to logical ends; avoid discursiveness and perversion of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The criticism that Sir James Frazer is unable to pursue to their logical ends the problems he proposes ... The charge of discursiveness ... and lastly he is tacitly charged with perversion of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure arguments are carried through consistently and coherently; avoid wandering discursions that obscure conclusions; present and interpret evidence honestly without selective distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat myths primarily as narratives/primitive science, not necessarily as religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths are not like psalms or hymns... They are narratives... They are to us obviously or demonstrably untrue and often irrational; on the other hand, they were to their first audience so reasonable as to appear truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse myths as narrative forms that can function as explanation, entertainment, or primitive knowledge rather than equating myth automatically with religious feeling or dogma. Distinguish different kinds of myth (etiological, entertaining, god-myths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider that ritual often generates myths (etiology)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sound method ... to assume that for the most part it is the ritual that generates the myth, and not the myth the ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exploring the origin of myths associated with ceremonies, prioritize investigating the ritual practices and social institutions that may have given rise to explanatory stories, rather than assuming myths precede rites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize myths about gods as a primary vehicle of religious belief
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one class of myth--that which deals with the gods--has probably more influence upon the popular acceptance and spread of religious ideas of a primitive type than either dogma or ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give special analytical weight to god-myths when studying religious formation and transmission, as they may shape popular theological understanding more than formal doctrine or ritual alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess 'religiousness' by experiential feeling (awe) as well as doctrinal categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of religiousness attaches ... far less in virtue of any one of these ideal constructions, than in virtue of that basic feeling of awe which drives a man ... into personal relations with the supernatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the religious character of practices and myths by considering emotional and experiential dimensions (awe, personal relation to supernatural) rather than relying solely on typological labels like animism or animatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a 'test of recurrence' but remain cautious about its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the tale bear a strong resemblance in more than one of its circumstances to any other tradition or group of traditions? If so, it should be a comparatively simple matter to judge to which group it belongs ... Our 'test of recurrence' is not always sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recurrence (cross-tradition similarity) to classify a tale as myth/folklore/history, but be alert to exceptions where myths group with folklore or vice versa; corroborate recurrence with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate written traditions in light of oral transmission and dating
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional narrative ... was not written down by contemporary or nearly contemporary authority. Before it had become a written document it had lived long as oral tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using texts as evidence, trace their oral antecedents and the chronology of recording; consider that a written record may be a later compilation of long-standing oral tradition and assess its value accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overstate local cults into presumed state mythologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor A.B. Cook ... has collected material to prove the existence throughout Europe of a sky-god... but he elevates this cult into something resembling a state mythology, and we have no record of any such state religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extrapolating from regional or fragmentary cult evidence to claims of unified, state-level religion without supporting records; beware of overgeneralisation from diffuse data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative studies' dependence on secondhand sources is not inherently blameworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The criticism that Sir James Frazer's great work 'second-hand' ... in comparative mythology the facts collated must of necessity be gleaned from the writings of others. This cry is surely unsuitable to mythological debate!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that large-scale comparative syntheses often rely on secondary literature; judge such works on the quality of selection, critical appraisal, and synthesis rather than dismissing them solely for using others' reports.
